pages.title: Noren Curtains
pages.text: Noren are the split curtains that hang in doorways. Cut a block of wool on the stonecutter to get one in that color, or dye an existing noren instead: the dye changes the color and the pattern is kept. Four patterns exist — plain, striped, wavy and long — in all 16 wool colors, and the long one hangs four blocks further down. Place one against a wall face to hang it there.

pages.title: Plank Walls
pages.text: Plank walls are wall blocks in every wood type, cut two at a time from the matching planks on the stonecutter. They fill a whole block, boarded on the sides and plain planks on top, and they do not join to each other on their own: lay them down one block at a time.

pages.title: Glazed Tiles
pages.text: Tiles come in seven colors: cyan, orange, yellow, brown, blue, black and gray. They are glazed the way terracotta is stained: put a dye in the middle of eight deepslate tiles and you get eight tiles in that color. Every color has a full block, stairs, a slab and a vertical slab, which is a half-height piece standing against the wall you click. The three shapes come off the tile block on the stonecutter.

pages.title: Paper and Shoji
pages.text: Two paper-faced building blocks, each in a solid form and a thin pane form. The shoji frame is paper stretched over a lattice of sticks; the paper window is the plainer sheet beside it, the same shape with a border instead of a grid. Both are cheap — sticks and paper — and both stonecut into four panes, while a block of panes crafts into sixteen. They let light through rather than blocking it, so a room walled with them stays bright, and they burn as fuel if you are ever desperate enough for paper to do it.

pages.title: Lanterns
pages.text: Four paper lanterns, red and white, plain or lettered, and all of them lit brightly enough to light a whole room on their own. They turn to face you as you place them, and the lettered pair turns its written side out toward you as well. Set one on top of another and the lower lantern switches to its hanging model by itself, so a column of them reads as a single string. There is no recipe for them; look for them in the houses.
